Embassies on alert as Iran ramps up threats, U.S. elections loom
U.S. embassy officials in the Middle East were on high alert as new reports said Iran is in "advanced stages" of planning attacks against Americans.
The alerts followed the U.S. order for non-emergency government employees to leave Saudi Arabia this week.
The Trump administration has vowed renewed military strikes on Iran after the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3.
The U.S. embassy HQ in Riyadh is pictured on March 3, 2026.
U.S. embassy officials were on heightened alert around the Middle East as new reports said Iran is in the "advanced stages" of planning attacks against Americans Friday.
A memo from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said agencies received intelligence that Iran has "substantially increased efforts to target U.S. personnel" in the region, according to a New York Times report , and that the threats applied to "certain other countries" as well.
The warnings come after the U.S. ordered non-emergency government employees to leave Saudi Arabia this week, as attacks from the Iran-backed Houthis have worsened and the broader war between the U.S. and Tehran nears its eighth month.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it destroyed two ballistic missiles fired by the group, aimed towards Taif and Yanbu.
Despite rising tensions, an Iranian official told The Associated Press on Saturday that Tehran remains open to talks with the U.S. under the former Pakistan-brokered deal that was agreed to in June.
Reza Amiri Moghadam, Iran's ambassador to Islamabad, said Iranian officials are prepared to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if the Trump administration lifts its naval blockade, AP reported, but he said Washington has rebuffed the proposal. Later in the day, Iranian state media denied the report.
The Trump administration has vowed to put off military strikes on Iran after the midterm elections on Nov. 3, as the fallout from the war in Iran has caused a major disruption in the U.S. economy — with inflation and affordability the top concerns for voters who will decide control of Congress early next month.
Rising Middle East tensions sent oil prices soaring this week. Benchmark Brent crude futures topped $116 a barrel, a six-month high . U.S. West Texas Intermediate rose 3.8% to settle over $103 a barrel.

SUNRAY, Texas (KVII) — The City of Sunray has over-odorized its natural gas system, which could cause a stronger-than-normal gas smell in the area, the Sunray Volunteer Fire Department said.
The department urged residents to use caution and not assume a strong odor is harmless because of the over-odorization.
Natural gas is odorless in its natural state. Utilities add an odorant to help people detect gas leaks . The odorant smells similar to rotten eggs.
If you smell gas indoors, leave the building and move to a safe location. Do not operate electrical switches, use open flames or do anything that could create a spark. The fire department also advised residents to open windows and call 911 from a safe location if the odor persists or they have concerns.

items.content:
Energy Transfer vs. Kinder Morgan: Which Natural Gas Pipeline Stock Is the Better Buy for the AI Power Boom?
Energy Transfer (TXSE: ET) and Kinder Morgan (NYSE: KMI) are two of the largest midstream businesses in North America. Although both have cut their dividends in the past, they are growing them at a steady clip today. However, as artificial intelligence (AI) shifts the demand story in the electricity sector, Kinder Morgan is likely the better-positioned business, if you're willing to pay for it. Here's what you need to know to choose between these two midstream operators.
There is a massive effort underway to build the infrastructure that supports artificial intelligence . However, at its core, AI is just a fancy computer program. It doesn't exist without electricity. The more AI infrastructure that's built, the more electricity is needed. Between 2024 and 2030, the International Energy Agency expects electricity demand from AI to increase "more than four times faster than the growth of total electricity consumption from all other sectors."
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
Image source: Getty Images. The world needs more electricity in a big way, with some estimates that electricity demand will grow by 60% between 2025 and 2045. That's up from growth of just 10% between 2005 and 2025. Pipeline companies are a vital part of supplying this electricity because natural gas is increasingly being used to generate power.
There's more good news. Businesses like Energy Transfer and Kinder Morgan largely charge fees for the use of their energy infrastructure assets. So while commodity prices can be highly volatile, midstream companies largely sidestep that risk. The volume flowing through their systems is more important than the price of what is being moved. In other words, Energy Transfer and Kinder Morgan are likely to benefit from AI regardless of what happens to natural gas prices.
Which is better positioned: Energy Transfer or Kinder Morgan?
There is a notable difference between Energy Transfer and Kinder Morgan regarding natural gas. Natural gas makes up around 35% of Energy Transfer's business, while Kinder Morgan's exposure is 67%. In fact, Kinder Morgan claims to own the largest natural gas transmission network in the United States.
From this perspective, Kinder Morgan is better positioned to benefit from increasing demand for the natural gas used to generate electricity. If that is all you are focused on, it is probably the better choice for your portfolio.
The problem is that Kinder Morgan's dividend yield is only 3.4%, which is far below the 6.7% yield that you could collect from Energy Transfer. To buy either for a dividend portfolio, you need to accept that both have both cut their dividends in the past. They are growing again, as noted above. Syria's Energy Comeback Could Reshape Middle East Oil and Gas
Syria is undergoing countrywide reconstruction after more than a decade of conflict, which caused extensive infrastructure damage and led to millions of people being displaced. As Syrians rebuild their lives, the government has big plans for economic diversification and growth to support long-term recovery. Thanks to its favourable geographic position, this includes the development of a strong energy sector that could help eventually establish Syria as a regional hub.
Syria is now led by President Ahmed al-Sharaa, who formed a transitional government on March 29, 2025, following the end of the Assad regime. The government has introduced a wide range of policies and reforms over the past year, across all sectors, aimed at improving living standards and supporting economic growth. The national strategy focuses on institutional reorganisation, security integration, economic stabilisation, and transitional justice ahead of planned national elections in 2030.
The transitional government has taken control over Syrian energy, including the Omar oil field and Tabiyeh gas complex. This follows over a decade during which Syria's energy sector was split, with Damascus situated far from the country's oil-rich northeast. For years, while the government still oversaw gas output in the country's central region, it lost control of some of the country's largest production sites.
A 2026 agreement between the transitional government and the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) provides the potential to integrate SDF forces into state structures, which could further unify energy governance. Meanwhile, the lifting of United States and European Union sanctions on Syria, following the fall of the Assad regime, and the relaunch of the SWIFT transfer system have made it easier for international companies to invest in Syria.
Before the conflict, which commenced in 2011, Syria was producing an average of 380,000 bpd of crude and 900 million cubic feet of gas. However, the conflict dramatically reduced output, with oil production down 80 per cent and gas by half, according to figures from Wood Mackenzie. Nevertheless, Syria is still home to estimated reserves of 1.3 billion barrels of oil equivalent, in addition to having vast unexplored onshore areas and an entirely untapped offshore sector. Higher levels of foreign investment could support an accelerated recovery in the oil and gas sector.
In May, Syria announced that it had an offshore site for its first deep-water oil and gas exploration project to be developed by the U.S. major Chevron, Qatar's UCC Holding, and the Syrian Petroleum Company (SPC). This supports the government's aim to attract greater foreign investment in Syria's energy sector. Other U.S. oil and gas firms have also expressed interest in Syrian oil and gas projects under the transitional government, opening the door to new investment opportunities.
There is significant potential for Syria's energy industry given the current geopolitical challenges to global energy. Iran's restrictions on energy trade through the Strait of Hormuz have spurred interest in Syria as a potential transit route for pipelines transporting Persian Gulf oil and gas to the Mediterranean. Syria's border with Turkey offers enhanced access to major pipeline networks, which could facilitate the transport of oil and gas from the Middle East to Europe. With greater investment, Syria could serve as an "energy land bridge" for Hormuz-bypass pipelines, according to the Baker Institute .
In addition to redeveloping its oil and gas assets and potentially acting as a regional energy trade hub, the transitional government also has major plans for Syria's renewable energy sector. Small-scale solar projects have already begun to emerge, with estimates suggesting that the country's off-grid solar capacity increased from around 250 MW in 2022 to over 2 GW in 2025.
Syria is looking to develop both its solar and wind power sectors. In June 2025, the government signed a $7 billion deal with a consortium from Qatar, Turkey, and the United States to rebuild its power sector, including four gas-fired power plants and a 1 GW solar park. The project is expected to add 5 GW of capacity, which will cover almost half of the current electricity demand.
The government signed a Joint Development Agreement with the Saudi energy group ACWA Power in September 2025, as they work to identify suitable locations for wind energy projects, aiming to develop 1 GW of solar PV capacity and approximately 1.5 GW of wind power, as well as utility-scale battery storage to enhance reliability.
In February, the Syrian Ministry of Energy also signed an agreement with the Dubai-based energy group Marv Energy to develop a 700-MW wind farm with plans to install 140 locally manufactured wind turbines across several sites to connect to the national electricity grid. Marv Energy plans to manufacture the turbines at its factory in the city of Homs in western Syria. It aims to complete the project within five to seven years.
In October, the Ministry of Energy issued a request for expressions of interest for the Halabiya-Zalabiya Dam project on the Euphrates River. The project would include the construction of an 81-MW hydropower plant and a 1.2-GW pumped-storage hydropower facility, with an estimated investment cost of $1.16 billion. The project would require the development of a 1,200-metre-long, 23-metre-high dam. Meanwhile, the hydropower plant would have three 27-MW turbines.
Syria has significant oil, gas, and renewable energy capacity, but it is highly dependent on foreign investment to support development. Due to ongoing limitations to energy trade via the Strait of Hormuz, several investors are looking to Syria to develop alternative trade routes between the Middle East and Europe, which could support the country's economic recovery.

items.title: Inflation, earnings reports and the mood of consumers and the Federal Reserve fill out a busy week - WTOP News
items.summary: Inflation, earnings reports and the mood of consumers and the Federal Reserve fill out a busy week  WTOP News
items.content:
NEW YORK (AP) — A key update on inflation and its impact on consumer confidence, economic growth and interest rate policy will fill a busy calendar this week along with more big earnings reports.
They all arrive just weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections that will determine the future makeup of Congress as the U.S. economy grapples with constantly shifting global trade conflicts and a global oil shortage brought on by the U.S. war with Iran. Inflation is stubbornly high, consumers are losing confidence and the resilient jobs market is showing more signs of stress.
Here’s a look at some of the key reports coming in the week ahead.
Consumer confidence keeps falling as inflation squeezes household budgets
Americans are losing confidence in the economy as rising prices for everything from gas to groceries guts budgets. The latest consumer confidence survey from business group The Conference Board on Tuesday is expected to show that consumer confidence kept shrinking in October.
The last report showed that confidence plunged in September to the lowest level in more than a decade. The October report is expected to show confidence kept weakening. Consumer confidence is down sharply from two years ago, according to the survey. In that time, the U.S. has waged a wide-ranging trade war with much of the world, including its neighbors and closest trading partners. The uncertainty around the sudden shifts in tariffs left businesses and consumers wary about planning ahead over worries about higher costs. The U.S. war with Iran that started in 2026 slashed global oil supplies and added more fuel to rising prices.
The Federal Reserve struggles to contain rising inflation
The Federal Reserve will close out a two-day meeting on Wednesday and is expected to hold its benchmark interest rate steady following a hike at its September meeting. The central bank has been signaling that it is still worried about inflation and that it may have to continue raising rates to help tame rising costs. Wall Street still expects that one more rate hike is coming at the Fed's meeting in December.
Higher interest rates make borrowing more costly, which in turn can slow economic growth and cool stubbornly hot inflation. The Fed has to balance taming inflation with supporting the jobs market. Higher interest rates and slower economic growth could dampen rising inflation, but they could also hurt job growth at a time when the somewhat resilient employment market is showing signs of stress.
Economic growth faces the impact of stubborn inflation, weakening consumer confidence
The U.S. Department of Commerce on Thursday will release its initial report on economic growth during the third quarter and economists expect a sluggish result. Economists are forecasting that gross domestic product, which is the nation's output of goods and services, rose 1.7% from July through September. It's the first of three reports for third-quarter GDP and can be revised higher or lower.
The forecast for the initial assessment marks an easing from 2.2% growth during the second quarter . GDP growth has been slowing since the first quarter under pressure from higher oil prices fueling already stubbornly high inflation. Growth has been bolstered by a strong stock market and businesses investing in artificial intelligence technology. Households, though, have been struggling with higher costs on everything from gas to groceries eating up more of their budgets at the same time that average wages for workers stagnate.
Inflation keeps heating up as US war with Iran squeezes global oil supplies
The latest inflation update is expected to show that prices on everything from gasoline to clothing and groceries marched higher at a faster rate in September. The U.S. will release the personal consumption expenditures report, or PCE, on Thursday and economists expect that inflation jumped at a 3.7% rate, up from a 3.4% rate in August.
The PCE is the preferred measure of inflation used by the Fed, which wants to bring inflation down to its target rate of 2%. Several other measures of inflation have also moved stubbornly above a 3%. Inflation has been rising at an even sharper rate since the U.S. war with Iran started in February, essentially shutting down the vital Strait of Hormuz and stifling the global oil supply. That has prompted a surge in gasoline prices that have been a direct hit to household budgets . Higher diesel fuel costs raised the cost of shipping and warehousing goods, which businesses typically pass along to consumers.
The latest updates on retail sales show that household spending remains strong, on the surface. Much of that spending, though, is the result of paying higher costs , especially for gasoline.
Corporate earnings reports could shed light on AI investments and household spending
Investors have another busy week of earnings ahead, with reports from big names that could provide more insight on plans for AI spending and how inflation is influencing profits.
The most closely-watched reports this week are likely to be the big technology or technology-related companies that have seen their stock values surge as they heavily invest in artificial-intelligence technology with hopes for a big benefit. Google's parent company Alphabet reports its results on Wednesday, with Intel and Amazon reporting their latest results on Thursday. Analysts expect all three companies to report profit gains as Wall Street tries to determine whether their big AI investments will translate into future growth and whether their outsized stock values are justified.
A wide range of other companies will report results this week, shedding more light on inflation's impact across industries. Shipping company UPS and beverage giant Coca-Cola report results on Tuesday. Starbucks reports its results on Thursday, while oil giants Exxon Mobil and Chevron report their results on Friday.

items.title: Two rescued after Nairobi building collapse with five still missing
items.summary: Police have launched a manhunt for the building's owner and contractor after the multi-storey building collapsed while still under construction.
items.content:
Two people have been pulled alive from the rubble of a building that collapsed in Kenya's capital, Nairobi, on Friday, as a search continues for five still missing.
Police said on Saturday that a manhunt had been launched for the building's owner and the contractor responsible for the site.
Dramatic footage shows the bottom floor of the block, thought to have been 16 or 18 storeys, giving way before the rest of the building crumples, sending a plume of dust into the surrounding streets.
Dozens of builders had been working on the upper floors when it collapsed, but managed to emerge largely unscathed. Those missing were thought to have been in shops at the base of the building.
The incident has raised fresh concerns about construction standards and regulations in Kenya.
The block was under construction when it collapsed on Friday afternoon, with footage showing scaffolding still wrapped around the outside of the building. Officials said 11 shops had already opened on the bottom floors.
Interior ministry official Kipchumba Murkomen said 66 of the 67 construction workers in the building at the time had been able to get out unharmed, while the other had suffered injuries that were not life-threatening.
On Friday, Murkomen said that seven people had been reported missing and rescue teams had made contact with some of those trapped beneath the rubble.
The two survivors rescued on Saturday have been taken to hospital, police said.
Images from the scene, in Nairobi's Eastleigh area, show the concrete floors of the building piled on top of one another, as rescue workers saw through metal to get to those believed to have been stuck underneath.
Image caption, Footage taken from nearby shows moments before (left) and moments after (right) the building collapsed
Questions have emerged about why the building suddenly collapsed and whether it met planning regulations.
Kenya's National Construction Authority said in a statement that it had identified the company behind the development, as well as the architect and structural engineer, but did not say whether the site had been inspected before Friday.
The National Police Service said it had launched an investigation to establish the cause of the collapse and determine whether anyone was criminally liable.
In a statement it warned that anyone found responsible for negligence or violating building regulations would "face the full force of the law".
Nairobi Governor Sakaja Johnson told local media that the owners of the building did not have the required paperwork for the building to be occupied.
He urged the national government to give local authorities greater powers to penalise "developers who disregard approved building plans and safety standards".
Building collapses are not uncommon in Nairobi, with poor construction or improper planning often cited as contributing factors.

items.title: Man arrested after fire at Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat
items.summary: Some 200 emergency personnel were deployed to fight the blaze at the Nazi dictator's Alpine residence in Germany.
items.content:
Figure caption, Watch as fire engulfs Hitler's mountaintop retreat
Police in the southern German state of Bavaria have detained a 33-year-old German man during a fire at Adolf Hitler's Alpine mountain retreat, the Kehlsteinhaus, also known as the Eagle's Nest.
Dispatchers in Traunstein received a fire alarm from the building at 21:15 local time (19:15 GMT) on Friday and firefighters found it engulfed in flames.
Some 200 emergency personnel were deployed to the scene where the blaze was still burning early on Saturday, as police said difficult terrain hindered efforts to bring the fire under control.
Police said they apprehended the man riding a motorcycle near the scene, German media reported. A criminal investigation has been launched.
There is currently nothing to suggest the involvement of further suspects, police official Gerhart Holzinger told a press conference on Saturday afternoon.
Public prosecutor Rainer Vietze said a psychiatric report had concluded the 33-year-old man showed signs of possible mental illness and diminished responsibility might therefore be assumed.
Vietze said a possible political motive was also being considered, but stressed the investigation was in its early stages.
The residence, above the town of Berchtesgaden, was one of several buildings in the area used by the Nazi dictator and his entourage during World War Two.
Hitler and top Nazi officials used his nearby Berghof residence to plan the invasion of the USSR in 1941 and the whole complex was considered one of his headquarters.
He also used the area as a backdrop for propaganda films portraying him as a lover of animals and nature.
Local media reported that site had been "largely destroyed" and the public was urged to avoid the area.
Bavaria's Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann told reporters that the site would "under no circumstances remain a ruin", broadcaster BR24 reported. "It is important that we continue our work of remembrance," he added.
Image caption, The retreat was seen smouldering on Saturday morning
Completed by the Nazis in 1938, the Eagle's Nest, which sits at an elevation of around 1,800m (5,900ft), escaped destruction after their defeat in 1945.
Since then, it has become a popular tourist destination and houses a mountain inn.
It serves as "a cautionary reminder of the abysses of the inhumane Nazi dictatorship", according to its official website , external .
During WW2, Hitler and his followers were responsible for the deaths of tens of millions of people, including the mass murder of European Jews. Homosexuals, gypsies, the disabled and ethnic minorities were sent to concentration camps and put to death.
There has been a wider debate in Germany and Vienna over whether to preserve, repurpose or demolish buildings connected to Hitler.
While some say these buildings should be preserved for historical reasons, others have raised concerns that they could be used as monuments or places of pilgrimage for neo-Nazis and far-right extremists.
In June, Berlin authorities announced they would tear down one of Hitler's bunkers - described at the time as "the power centre of Nazi Germany" - to build flats and offices on the site.
Those critical of the plans said the bunker had "significant historical value" and that it should have been turned into a museum and memorial site with an exhibit about the end of the war.
And in July, after years of controversy, Austrian authorities refurbished the house in the town of Braunau am Inn in which Hitler was born and turned it into a police station.

items.title: Can Amazon Take Market Share From Nvidia in the AI Chip Race? - The Motley Fool
items.summary: Can Amazon Take Market Share From Nvidia in the AI Chip Race?  The Motley Fool
items.content:
Amazon ( AMZN -0.95% ) recently launched a new software tool that will allow its custom Trainium AI chips to run code written in the most popular AI coding language without modification. It's a move aimed at boosting the potential for Amazon's custom application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) to take market share away from Nvidia 's ( NVDA -0.59% ) widely used graphics processing units as demand for AI chips continues to swell.
Amazon isn't the only tech giant working on its own AI chips for commercial use. Alphabet  recently began making its custom AI chips available for sale directly to enterprises, rather than limiting them to being leased through Google Cloud. However, investors shouldn't expect these developments to have a meaningful effect on Nvidia's financial results.
Amazon's AI chip business wrapped up the second quarter with a $25 billion annual revenue run rate. That's not small, but it pales in comparison to the $96.2 billion in revenue Nvidia booked in its fiscal 2027 second quarter alone, or the more than $300 billion it booked over the past four quarters.

While Amazon's push to commercialize its custom chips could boost sales, the largest tech companies are still rushing to buy Nvidia chips. That's how Nvidia managed to produce 106% year-over-year revenue growth in its most recent quarter, and CEO Jensen Huang says that AI demand is still accelerating.
If anything, Amazon's AI chips can become niche hardware in the industry. Since the AI build-out has been so expansive, it may provide enough room for high, sustained revenue growth rates. If Amazon's chip business can generate net profit margins similar to Nvidia's, that should be enough to boost Amazon's stock price.
Another point supporting the view that Amazon's AI chips won't significantly impact Nvidia's business is that Amazon is still buying Nvidia chips. In fact, it has built up a stockpile of billions of dollars' worth of them that it doesn't yet have the data center infrastructure and connected electricity supply to power up.
Nvidia's processors have become the most reliable option for providing high-end compute in an industry that values speed and will pay a premium for flawless execution. Even as Amazon touts the value of its own chips for the narrower workloads they are designed to handle, for flexible compute power, the tech leader still turns to Nvidia.
Notably, those stockpiled supplies of chips and data center servers highlight that electrical supplies will remain a major bottleneck for AI infrastructure expansion. Still, hyperscalers aren't waiting for that problem to be resolved completely, and continue to accelerate their capital expenditures.
Nvidia's guidance implies that its business is still growing at a substantial rate despite the intensifying competition. Its fiscal 2027 third-quarter guidance calls for $108 billion in revenue at the midpoint, which would amount to 12.3% sequential growth. That guidance supports Huang's claim that AI demand is accelerating.
While more rivals are likely to enter the expanding AI chip market, Nvidia remains the clear leader in data center chips.

Philips helped Taiwan begin its decades-long technology transformation
Li Kwoh-ting pursued foreign expertise to build Taiwan's domestic electronics industry
TSMC manufactures advanced chips, while ASML builds equipment used in production
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has recently discussed how Taiwan's semiconductor leadership emerged through decades of industrial partnerships, government planning and manufacturing expertise.
During a recent conversation with Lex Fridman, Huang discussed how European technology relationships helped establish capabilities that later supported Taiwan's electronics industry.
The island now manufactures more than 90% of the world's most advanced semiconductors, giving its relatively small territory enormous importance to global technology supply chains.
Philips helped establish Taiwan's electronics foundations
The story dates back to the 1950s, when Taiwanese economic planner Li Kwoh-ting pursued foreign partnerships to develop domestic manufacturing technology.
His efforts included attracting Dutch electronics manufacturer Philips, whose involvement helped introduce industrial knowledge and production capabilities into Taiwan's developing electronics sector.
Philips subsequently became part of the historical background behind companies that helped shape semiconductor manufacturing and equipment development.
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) eventually became central to advanced chip production, while Dutch equipment supplier ASML emerged as a leading manufacturer of lithography systems.

These businesses occupy different positions within semiconductor supply chains, with TSMC fabricating integrated circuits and ASML supplying machinery used during chip production.
Their historical connections to Philips help explain how international industrial relationships contributed to Taiwan's technological development.
However, their subsequent success involved different corporate histories, investments and technological advances rather than one partnership determining the industry's eventual direction.
Taiwan's manufacturing capabilities developed through sustained industrial expansion, foreign relationships and growing demand for increasingly sophisticated electronic components.
Computer manufacturing created another opportunity for Taiwan
Taiwan's electronics industry continued expanding as international demand for personal computers created new opportunities for component suppliers.
IBM helped accelerate this development when it published specifications for its personal computer architecture, enabling other manufacturers to build compatible machines and supporting components.
Taiwanese businesses capitalised on the growing market by designing chipsets and supplying computer components to manufacturers.
TSMC and United Microelectronics Corporation (UMC) subsequently became important semiconductor manufacturers, although their expansion involved distinct strategies and developments across the industry.
The growth of compatible personal computers also created opportunities for motherboard suppliers serving companies assembling and selling complete systems.
Michael Dell , who founded his computer business during this period, initially built machines using commercially available components, including parts sourced through international supply chains.
Taiwanese suppliers formed part of that developing network, although Dell's eventual success also depended on his direct sales approach and business operations.
IBM's influence therefore represents a separate stage in Taiwan's industrial development, rather than a direct consequence of Philips' earlier involvement.
Huang's account connects foreign investment, manufacturing expertise and changing market opportunities to explain Taiwan's rise within the semiconductor industry.
Its current leadership, however, rests on decades of further investment, engineering advances and specialised production capabilities.
The island's concentration of advanced chip manufacturing has become particularly significant as AI increases demand for sophisticated processors .
Governments and technology companies are consequently seeking reliable supplies, while Taiwan's manufacturing expertise remains difficult to reproduce quickly elsewhere.

items.content:
Will the Fed raise interest rates this year? Divided economists weigh in
The central bank has held interest rates steady five consecutive times.
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh this week struck a combative tone about inflation, but the central bank opted against deploying its most powerful weapon: An interest rate hike .
"The path to central bank heaven means delivering on our remit," Warsh told reporters in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday afternoon. "This is the right team to win the battle against high inflation."
The remarks came minutes after the central bank issued its decision to hold interest rates steady for a fifth consecutive time, though pressure for a rate hike seemed to be building within its ranks.
Chair of the Federal Reserve Kevin Warsh speaks during a news conference at the William McChesney Martin Jr. Federal Reserve Board Building in Washington, July 29, 2026.
Three of the 12 members on the Fed's policymaking board voted in favor of a rate hike, marking the largest number of dissenters casting ballots in the same direction since 2016.
After the announcement, economists appeared as divided as the policymakers, underscoring the uncertain prospects for a rate hike by the end of this year.
Some analysts told ABC News they expect a rate increase as soon as the Fed's next meeting in September, pointing to risks posed by price increases as global oil shortage shows little sign of letting up.
Others cast doubt on whether the Fed will raise rates at all over the remainder of 2026, noting an apparent willingness on the part of Warsh to let the market push borrowing costs higher without a nudge from the central bank.
What interest rate hikes mean for you and the economy
"Uncertainty and volatility are a feature and not a bug," Joseph Brusuelas, global economist at RSM, said in a note to investors about Warsh's stated preference that investors respond to economic events rather than Fed policy statements.
"This has turned out to be anything but a boring and uneventful summer," Brusuelas added.
The Iran war triggered a historic oil shortage that drove up fuel costs and catapulted inflation to a three-year high in May, the same month Warsh took the helm of the central bank.
A preliminary peace agreement in June offered up some relief , but a burst of on-again, off-again fighting in recent weeks has caused crude prices to rise again.
Elevated price increases pose a challenge for central bankers eager to beat back price hikes. In theory, the Fed could raise interest rates in an effort to cool off prices, but the move risks a slowdown of hiring.
Oil prices surge after Trump vows retaliation for Iranian attack
Fortunately, hiring has proven largely resilient, despite increased costs borne by shoppers and businesses.
Odds of a quarter-point rate hike at the Fed's next meeting in September stand at 63%, according to the CME Group's FedWatch Tool , a measure of investor sentiment. Odds of a rate hike by the end of the year stand at 83%.
Woman's body found in massive tank after yearslong investigation
Minnesota man credited with saving kids, school bus driver surprised with check
2 dead, 11 injured after Kansas mother drives onto soccer field during game: Police
"I do think we're going to see a rate hike. Maybe not at the next meeting but at some time in 2026," Rebel Cole, a professor of finance at Florida Atlantic University who formerly worked at the Federal Reserve, told ABC News. "Inflation won't come down until oil prices do. The Fed is boxed in."
Some economists, by contrast, questioned whether the Fed would raise interest rates over the remainder of the year.
The Fed holds little capacity to address inflation driven by supply shortages, such as the current oil shock, Brusuelas said. Higher interest rates would instead reduce demand as shoppers and businesses weather expensive borrowing costs. The Fed may instead expect inflation to fall once oil supply returns, Brusuelas said.
"We think that the nature of the supply shock and the Fed's tendency to look through such shocks implies that the Fed has the space to keep the policy rate on hold," Brusuelas added.
Fed holds interest rates steady as economy weathers resurgent inflation
Warsh, meanwhile, has said he wants to let investors set the cost of borrowing in the market for short- and long-term bonds, instead of taking a strong hand himself through public statements or policy prescriptions.
In a sense, that approach has worked, some economists said. The 30-year Treasury yield hit its highest level since 2007 on Wednesday, after the Fed issued its rate decision.
The average interest rate on a 30-year fixed mortgage, which closely tracks the 10-year Treasury yield, stands at 6.66%, its highest level in a year, Freddie Mac data on Thursday showed.
"That market-delivered tightening is why the Fed could hold," Gordon Johnson, CEO and founder of data firm GLJ Research, told ABC News in a statement. "The market did the work; Warsh banked it."
A wide gap between the benchmark rate set by central bankers, the federal funds rate, and the market for Treasuries could pose challenges for policymakers, however. Investors may seek to exploit the gap, and economic tumult could result, Gerald Epstein, a professor of economics at the University of Massachusetts, Amherst, told ABC News.
"Eventually, the Fed would need to raise interest rates," Epstein said.
Too much focus on wonky economic questions risks overlooking the political dynamic surrounding interest rate policy, some economists said.
President Donald Trump pressured Warsh's predecessor, Jerome Powell, in an effort to reduce interest rates. The Department of Justice opened an unprecedented criminal probe into Powell, which he viewed as part and parcel of the pressure campaign. Trump has denied any involvement in the probe, which the DOJ later dropped .
Warsh has voiced support for the independence of the Fed, but he may seek to avoid rate increases even as he vows to fight inflation, especially as the political calendar barrels toward the November midterm elections, Epstein said.
"The elephant in the room is that the hawkish tone of the Fed chair is at odds with the preference of the White House for a rate cut," Brusuelas said.

items.title: Palestinian families displaced as Israeli forces demolish Hebron homes
items.summary: The crackdown follows the killing of two Israeli soldiers by two Palestinian gunmen on Friday - and comes just days ahead of Israel's election.
items.content:
Image caption, More than 200 families have been displaced, Palestinian officials say
The Israeli military has launched a sweeping crackdown in the occupied West Bank, demolishing homes and businesses in the city of Hebron and displacing hundreds of families, according to local officials.
Footage shared online showed destruction caused by Israeli bulldozers, with at least one whole street appearing to have been flattened. The military has also cordoned off the city, heavily restricting the movement of its 200,000 residents.
The operation was announced by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday, in response to the killing of two Israeli soldiers by two Palestinian gunmen in an attack on a checkpoint. Three other Israeli soldiers were injured, and the gunmen were also killed.
Netanyahu said on Friday that buildings around the site of the attack and the neighbourhoods that the two gunmen were from would be "destroyed".
Hebron's Mayor Youssef al-Jaabari said more than 1,000 people had been displaced by the operation, which centred on the Ein Deir Baha and Farsh al-Hawa neighbourhoods, and targeted homes, businesses, industrial sites and infrastructure.
He said dozens of families had been forced to spend the night outside, with some told to leave without taking their vehicles, while homes were marked for demolition with spray paint.
He added that he believed the military planned to displace a total of 2,500 people from about 0.35 sq km of urban land. The city's governor and deputy mayor meanwhile said at least 200 families had been displaced.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) did not respond immediately to the BBC's request for comment. It said in a statement on social media that it had dozens of targets across the West Bank and that its operations would last for several days.
Image caption, Wreckage was seen around the site of Friday's shooting following demolitions by Israeli forces
Image caption, Bulldozers began demolitions on Friday afternoon
Image caption, Photos of one of the suspected gunmen in Friday's attack were shared by AFP news agency
Slide 1 of 3 , Sandy land around checkpoint. Wreckage in the distance. , Wreckage was seen around the site of Friday's shooting following demolitions by Israeli forces End of image gallery
It is common practice for Israeli forces to demolish the homes of Palestinians who are suspected of carrying out attacks on Israelis in the West Bank - a practice Israeli rights groups have criticised as collective punishment.
Netanyahu likened the operation to previous operations in Palestinian refugee camps in the north of the territory, when the Israeli military demolished hundreds of homes and displaced tens of thousands in 2025.
Friday's shooting came during a tense time for the region, with Israel's general election taking place in four days' time.
Netanyahu - who has built his campaign on the promise of security - cancelled his party's campaign events for Friday morning and headed to Hebron, wearing protective armour and posting a video on social media from the scene.
"We will evacuate the residents, go house to house, remove the weapons we find there, and deal with and destroy all terrorist infrastructure," he said.
He also announced he had reviewed plans for the largest military operation in the West Bank since 1967 - though did not say when it could be carried out. It is not clear whether the ongoing Hebron operation forms part of that.
In an interview with Israel's i24 television channel released on Saturday, he threatened "a very big surprise" for the Palestinian Authority (PA), which governs parts of the territory.
In a statement, the PA called for "urgent international action that went beyond condemnation" to prevent further forced displacement.
Meanwhile, his far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for Israel to launch a campaign in the West Bank "exactly like in Gaza or Lebanon," while far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir called for Israel to dismantle the PA.
Speaking to journalists, Hebron's mayor said the operation was "driven by the elections," and that Netanyahu and his ministers were attempting to secure the votes of the far-right and the settlers.

Fallow in St James's Market, London. The restaurant’s owners have signed a deal to open a branch in the Gulf. Photograph: Sophia Evans/The Observer

No unions, low taxes: why some of Britain’s top chefs are opening outposts in Gulf states
Leading restaurateur says Gulf countries actively help businesses set up, while east Asia has a better work ethic
Some of London’s top restaurants are opening branches in Dubai because of a “tax tsunami” in the UK and better work ethic abroad, according to a leading restaurateur.
James Robson, a co-owner of Fallow in St James’s Market, regarded as the capital’s hottest restaurant, serving 1,000 people a day, has just signed a deal to open an outpost in the Gulf.
Other restaurants have opened in Dubai , including the celebrity hotspot Scott’s in Mayfair, the two Michelin-starred Indian venue Gymkhana, and the upmarket Chinese restaurant Park Chinois. Isabel’s, a Mayfair institution enjoyed by politicians, has opened in Abu Dhabi. And the trendy Borough Market bakery Bread Ahead has branched out in Dubai.
Despite conflicts in the Middle East, including the US-Israeli war in Iran which caused Dubai to face bombardment and an exodus of expats earlier this year, restaurants continue to open in the emirate.
Speaking from Hong Kong, where he is looking at opportunities in Asia, Robson said: “East Asia, the States and the Gulf are key growth targets for us. America champions business, the Gulf actively encourages and assists, whilst east Asia has a work ethic and taxation system that puts the UK to shame. I’m incredibly keen to start working in these regions over the next few years.”
Fallow has risen to fame partially through Instagram, where it has 650,000 followers, and its striking dishes including a whole cod’s head drenched in a spicy butter sauce.
Restaurateurs have complained of the VAT rate for hospitality in the UK, which at 20% is one of the highest rates in Europe. The European average for restaurants is about 12%. In Italy, it is set at 10% for food sold in restaurants. Chefs are calling for Andy Burnham to use next week’s budget to cut the VAT rate.
Two-Michelin-starred Indian restaurant Gymkhana is one of several London establishments that has opened in Dubai Photograph: Sophia Evans/The Observer “We have had a tsunami of taxes that have got to the point where taking business risk simply does not make sense in the UK,” Robson said, “Sadly the country has sleepwalked into multiple anti-growth taxations the last two budgets and likely more will be forthcoming next week.”
The entrepreneur has asked for VAT to be put more in line with Europe. “Add 25% corporation tax and 40%-plus dividend tax, then you start to question why do businesses any more.”
Jason Atherton, a Michelin-starred chef, spends a third of his time at his Dubai restaurant now and says it is easier to make a profit abroad than in London.
But human rights experts have warned of exploitation and poor worker protections in the Gulf. Felix Jakens, Amnesty International UK’s director of campaigns, said: “Dubai might look like an attractive place to do business, but the UAE has a very poor record on workers’ rights and protection from labour exploitation. The UAE has spent heavily on polishing its image in the UK, not least through Manchester City, but that glamour shouldn’t distract from how the people who keep its economy running are treated.
“Migrant workers, who make up the majority of the UAE’s population, remain bound by a sponsorship system that ties them to their employers and exposes them to labour abuse. They are denied the right to form trade unions, leaving them few ways to challenge unfair treatment.
“Any UK business expanding into the Gulf has a responsibility to carry out proper human rights due diligence, to make sure the people working in its kitchens are treated fairly, paid properly and able to raise concerns without fear of losing their job or visa.”
The British Michelin-starred chef Jason Atherton has previously spoken out about high taxes and the UK’s struggling hospitality sector. Photograph: Richard Saker/The Guardian Some restaurants in Dubai are struggling: Dinner by Heston is temporarily closed and has been since the fallout from the war in the Middle East. The Michelin guide came under fire earlier this month because it included 16 restaurants that were either permanently or temporarily closed. It appears that some visits were undertaken by inspectors at the beginning of the year, before the war started.
Robson said he had no resentment paying UK tax. “I am incredibly proud of the taxes I pay and feel privileged that I can contribute to our country’s deficit and will continue to do so,” he said. “My point is UK growth simply does not have any risk-reward balance any more, therefore it’s play incredibly safe here and focus overseas.”

items.summary: As Nvidia has gone from chipmaker to industry financier, some investors see the company taking on outsized risk tied to the AI buildout.
items.content:
Nvidia's role as AI financier faces first big test as neoclouds take market hit
As Nvidia has transitioned from chipmaker to industry financier, some investors see the company taking on outsized risk tied to the AI buildout.
Those concerns are showing up in the market with shares of neoclouds tanking and bond yields rising.
"If the demand for compute doesn't meet these really super lofty expectations, we're going to have a problem," said David Trainer, founder and CEO of financial research firm New Constructs.
Jensen Huang, CEO of NVIDIA, presents new NVIDIA Vera Rubin DSX Pod Full-Stack Modular AI Factory as he gives a keynote address at the Berlin GPU Technology Conference (GTC) on October 21, 2026 in Berlin, Germany.
Nvidia's emergence as financier for the global AI buildout is facing its first major stress test as credit markets tighten for key partners.
After creating the chips that powered the early stages of the generative artificial intelligence era, Nvidia turned to using its financial prowess to fund AI model developers, data center companies and a host of so-called neoclouds. CEO Jensen Huang's strategy has been to not only build the most advanced technology but to provide customers with investment as well as help them take out loans so his systems can reach many more hands.
That's meant taking full advantage of Nvidia's investment grade credit rating and providing backstop guarantees on mega-projects for OpenAI so that buildouts can get funded at lower interest rates.
As of its last quarterly financial filing in July, Nvidia had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, in addition to its guarantee on up to $105 billion for chips, land and power at a proposed 10 gigawatt OpenAI data center in Ohio. The company signed as a tenant for $20 billion in future data center leases, which will later be assigned to third parties.
For the vast majority of these deals, Nvidia won't have to pay up unless participants in the project default.
"If the demand for compute doesn't meet these really super lofty expectations, we're going to have a problem," said David Trainer, founder and CEO of financial research firm New Constructs, in an interview.
Market conditions may soon test Nvidia's mettle. Shares of neoclouds CoreWeave , Nebius and IREN , all cash-burning companies in Nvidia's portfolio, are down at least 30% this month. CoreWeave, the biggest of the group, has seen the spread on its credit default swaps soar past 11%, as investors are forced to pay up for insurance against default.
Nvidia has backed other neoclouds that have run into challenges.
The company is an investor in Australian AI cloud provider Firmus, which abruptly withdrew its IPO plans this month, as well as Nscale out of the U.K. and SoftBank-backed SB Energy . Both of those companies filed to go public in the U.S. in September but haven't provided updates on their plans in weeks.
Nvidia wrapped up a third straight down week on Wall Street on Friday, with its stock now off 7.6% in October, on pace for its worst month since November of last year.
Huang reiterated his confidence in the market this week, telling CNBC on Thursday that demand for neoclouds is "off the charts."
"What is missing in the middle is the working capital to fuel that growth," Huang told CNBC's Arjun Kharpal on the sidelines of the company's GTC conference in Berlin. "Because there's just so much demand across so many sectors of AI, there's a scarcity of capital."
Nvidia has taken equity stakes in dozens of companies, including big investments in OpenAI and Anthropic. Its portfolio is worth $99 billion as of the second quarter.
Investors told CNBC that a big question surrounding Nvidia is how the company can use its cash and $5 trillion market cap to get more chips into customers' hands, and how much risk it will assume in the process.
Nvidia graphics processing units are critical for training and deploying AI models. Revenue in the latest fiscal year hit $216 billion, up roughly eightfold since OpenAI launched ChatGPT in late 2022.
Before the AI boom, Nvidia sold graphics cards that could fit into a standard server rack or PC. Its newest systems are much larger and more expensive. Nvidia's flagship Vera Rubin product is a seven-foot rack containing 72 GPUs and weighing as much as a pickup truck. It costs more than $7 million, according to a Morgan Stanley estimate.
While Nvidia still dominates the AI chip market, competition is emerging from the likes of Google , which rents out tensor processing units (TPUs) inside its massive cloud offering, and Advanced Micro Devices , which launched its first AI rack called Helios in July.
AMD rivals Nvidia with first AI system, signing Microsoft and Meta
Cash is Nvidia's other great advantage. The company generated $70 billion in free cash flow in the first half of this year, while AMD totaled just over $4 billion and Google parent Alphabet went cash flow negative in the second quarter to fund its buildout.
That's a big edge for Nvidia in building out its ecosystem. The company is now offering a full-service platform complete with software, services, integrated hardware and, for many customers, financing assistance.
Nvidia's most recent quarterly financial filing in August outlined over $500 billion in off-balance-sheet commitments over the coming years, with a majority maturing through fiscal 2029. That same month, Huang announced a partnership with six large asset managers on a $500 billion financing push designed to treat compute infrastructure as an asset class.
That agreement, which promised financial firms up to $125 billion in residual value guarantees on GPU financings, was in addition to the stakes Nvidia has taken as a limited partner in private equity funds. The company seeded $2 billion in Brookfield's inaugural AI Infrastructure Partners Fund, which aims to raise $10 billion in total capital, as well as other unconfirmed sums in KKR's Helix Digital Infrastructure (an $11 billion vehicle) and Valor Equity Partners' $5.4 billion dedicated compute fund.
"We used to build chips that we sell, and these are technology components that people buy and use," Huang told CNBC , in announcing the agreement in August. "But now, Nvidia's AI factory platform is really an investable asset."
Huang has adopted a marketing mantra to reinforce the unique value of its equipment.
"We're the most rentable. We're fungible, and we're durable," he said on a podcast with investor Brad Gerstner published last week.
While Nvidia waits for Wall Street firms to pull in investors to expand the GPU loan pool, the chipmaker is already actively fostering record-sized deals in the AI infrastructure space.
Nvidia's biggest single guarantee is for OpenAI's forthcoming facility in Pike County, Ohio, which could be the largest data center in the world. That deal requires use of Nvidia hardware for at least 20 years.
The shift from chips to capital carries significant risks should OpenAI run into trouble.
If OpenAI misses payments or faces insolvency, Nvidia can take over the lease, find a new tenant, or ask the landlord, SB Energy, to sell the facility, guaranteeing to pay the difference for the latter two arrangements up to $105 billion if the release or sale falls below a minimum price. Nvidia could also pay SB Energy a lump sum. On the other side, if OpenAI posts its own collateral, or achieves a high enough credit rating, Nvidia's guarantee ends.
At CoreWeave, Nvidia's investment includes equity and a commitment to buy up to $6.3 billion of its compute if it can't find another taker.
Nvidia's backstops can take many forms, such as guaranteeing a minimum resale price or a minimum hourly offtake price for the chips in the event the lender has to recoup the assets. With Sharon AI and other neoclouds, Nvidia's deals have come with revenue-sharing agreements.
"We believe these AI cloud partners have strong customer demand and robust sales pipelines but are constrained by the large-scale infrastructure that is required to meet that demand," Nvidia said in its quarterly filing.
Huang said this week that CoreWeave doesn't need Nvidia's backstop and that the neocloud's cost of capital is decreasing. CoreWeave has roughly $51.6 billion in total debt, including about $35 billion in notes, bonds and loans. Yields on its bonds maturing in 2031 and 2032 topped 15%.
Brian Stutland, portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, said the market jitters reflect concerns about the stability of the business.
CoreWeave and other neoclouds "will sign contracts into the future, and that all looks fine and dandy in their earnings reports, but is that contract going to be stable?" Stutland said. "Is it going to break at some point?"
Nvidia says its financial support can help customers build the infrastructure needed to meet strong demand for its chips. More computing capacity could also help AI labs develop new models and services, creating further demand for Nvidia products.
"They'll do $700 billion in revenue next year," Deepwater Asset Management founder Gene Munster told CNBC last month. "That affords them the ability to finance some of their customers."
Nvidia's credit backstops have mostly kicked in over the past six to 12 months. Its last annual filing , published in February, makes no mention of AI cloud agreements.
Warren Hosseinion, co-founder of AI infrastructure startup Compute Labs, said Nvidia doesn't want to be in the position of insurer, "but they're willing to play that role while the market and the industry catches up."
"They kind of control how things move," said Hosseinion, whose company tokenizes GPUs in order to open up pools of capital for neocloud operators. "They have to be very careful about how they release their technology at what pace, because a lot of that will dictate how the market moves around it."
Nvidia is actively looking for insurers to bear some of the risk associated with the potential loss in value of GPUs.
"Insurers are not yet a complete panacea to this problem," said Tom Hoad, executive director of product innovation at global insurance group Howden. "But they are probably going to turn up and be helpful in the right situations, and therefore open up some commercial transactions."
According to research from New Constructs, Nvidia's net present value of off-balance-sheet liabilities in fiscal 2026 totals over $153 billion, an increase of over $100 billion from last year.
Such liabilities have been growing across the entire AI trade, mainly in the form of lease obligations. Ratings agencies like Moody's have been sounding the alarm. In 2026, guarantees are the fastest-growing type of off-balance-sheet financing arrangements, the agency said.
Moody's doesn't count guarantees as debt when rating corporate buyers, but it's "something we're constantly monitoring," said David Gonzales, a vice president at the agency.
"These things are advanced structures that are unique, and so there is no blanket real approach you can take," he said. Gonzales said it's likely that chips will retain "values in excess of contractual residual value amounts" in the near future, which would mitigate risk in many of Nvidia's financing structures.
Still, how much exposure investment grade AI players can handle is "the question we're evaluating at all times every day," Gonzales said.
"It's the center of all of our discussions right now," he said.
— CNBC's Seema Mody contributed to this report.

items.title: If I Could Tell Every Investor 1 Thing About Stock Market Crashes, It Would Be This - The Motley Fool
items.summary: If I Could Tell Every Investor 1 Thing About Stock Market Crashes, It Would Be This  The Motley Fool
items.content:
With the bull market now nearly four years in, investors are bracing for some kind of reset.
The worst-case scenario would likely be a repeat of the dot-com bubble, in which the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite lost roughly 80% of its value between 2000 and 2002.
Many investors have cited similarities between what's going on now with artificial intelligence and the rise of the internet in the late 1990s.
In recent years, the market has gone through several major sell-offs, including the tariff storm in 2025, the market's reaction to rising interest rates in 2022, and the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.
There's no sugarcoating it: Those were not fun experiences and definitely felt stressful at the time. But if I could tell investors one thing about market crashes, it would be this.
Any long-term investors who think the past three or four years are the norm, where the market gains at least 15%, and often over 20%, would be sorely mistaken.
If you are a long-term investor with a five- to 10-year time horizon, expect a pullback. It may not necessarily be an event like the dot-com bubble. It could be a correction, in which the market falls by at least 10% from a recent peak, or a bear market, in which the market declines by at least 20%.
According to a Charles Schwab study published in 2025, there were 27 market corrections between November 1974 and February 2025, meaning there was a market correction roughly every other year during this period.
On six of those occasions -- 1980, 1987, 2000, 2007, 2020, and 2022 -- the broader benchmark S&P 500 ( ^GSPC -0.52% ) tipped into a bear market.
While it would certainly be nice for the market to grow like a weed every year, corrections and resets are actually what make a healthy market. Often, stocks or sectors soar unjustifiably due to investor enthusiasm and greed, ultimately becoming overvalued.
Those stocks need to reset to maintain market fundamentals and root out bad actors (not that poor performance necessarily means bad actors are involved).
Dips are also good for long-term investors because they allow them to buy stocks of very strong companies at a much better entry point, helping them accumulate more wealth over time. It's tougher to make money in a market where most companies always trade at premium valuations .
As I mentioned, a correction or bear market is never fun, especially if your portfolio is struggling. But the important thing to understand is that these crashes don't often last long.
For instance, according to Schwab, past bear markets tend to be much shorter than past bull markets. Dating back to 1961, past bear markets have averaged a 36% loss and lasted 409 days, or about 13 months.
Meanwhile, past bull markets have, on average, lasted 1,894 days, or slightly over five years, giving investors an average return of 182.5%.
What does this tell us? Those who grind through a bear market often eventually enter a bull market that more than makes up for losses incurred in the bear market.
If you don't believe me, just look back at the period since the 2020 pandemic. There have been two bear markets, and the S&P 500 has still generated fantastic gains.
As things stand, four years into a bull market, are we due for some kind of pullback? History suggests the answer is yes. But timing the market is next to impossible, so never try to.
The best thing you can do as an investor is to stay invested in the broader market and battle-test all your individual holdings. Make sure, to the best of your ability, that your investment thesis in a stock looks at what might happen to the company under tougher market or economic conditions.
It may not be a bad idea to have some cash ready to buy stocks if the market crashes.
